answer:
What I ran: a random circuit on 8 connected Garnet qubits (QB4, QB5, QB6, QB9, QB10, QB11, QB14, QB15). It has 10 layers. Each layer applies a random single-qubit gate to every qubit and then CZ gates on a random set of neighbouring pairs. After compiling it had 29 CZ gates. I ran it once with 1000 shots on garnet:mock (job 01a16062-40fa-76c1-b6b6-677fcb8b39f1, 0 credits). I worked out the exact ideal output probabilities on my laptop and scored the samples with linear XEB. Linear XEB is 2^n times the average ideal probability of the bitstrings you got, minus 1.

Numbers: xeb_ideal is 0.516. That is what a perfect quantum computer would score on this circuit. xeb_measured is -0.20 (-0.19 if you read the bit order the other way). This is not a real result. The mock device returns only 4 bitstrings, about 250 shots each, and they do not depend on the circuit. Its counts do not come from running the circuit, so it scores near or below zero. The mock only tests the plumbing. It cannot show quantum behavior.

What the score means: XEB is 1 when samples follow a fully scrambled ideal distribution. XEB is near 0 when samples are random noise, because a noise bitstring has an average ideal probability of 1/256. A real device with noise gives a value between 0 and the ideal. A score clearly above 0 shows the chip really ran this circuit. Google's 2019 result used this test. Our ideal value of 0.52 is below 1 because 8 qubits and 10 layers with few gates per layer does not fully scramble the circuit. A real Garnet run would be expected to land below 0.52, and I did not run it, so that is not a measurement.

Why 8 qubits is easy and 50 or more is not: to compute ideal probabilities, a laptop stores 2^n numbers. For 8 qubits that is 256 numbers, which takes microseconds. Each added qubit doubles it. At 50 qubits that is about 10^15 numbers, which is petabytes of memory, and at 60 it is far more than any computer can hold. Clever methods help but still scale badly for deep, well-mixed circuits. The XEB score needs those ideal probabilities, so checking a 50+ qubit device with it is only feasible when a supercomputer can still do the hard classical part. A quantum chip skips that cost because it just runs the circuit.
